summary:
Public Law 118-186 (enacted Dec. 23, 2024) expands the statutory responsibilities of the Science and Technology Directorate (S&T) within the Department of Homeland Security to enhance the detection and identification of illicit substances, particularly fentanyl and xylazine, at very low concentrations. The Act amends section 302 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. § 182) by adding a new paragraph (15) that directs S&T, in coordination with the Drug Enforcement Administration, to carry out research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analyses aimed at improving the safety, effectiveness, and efficiency of equipment and reference libraries used by federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement. The provision specifically authorizes work on: (A) portable detection equipment requiring minimal or no sample handling; (B) equipment capable of separating complex mixtures with low drug concentrations and high cutting-agent concentrations to extract signatures for field identification; and (C) technologies employing machine learning or artificial intelligence (as defined in 15 U.S.C. § 9401) and other techniques to predict whether substances are controlled substance analogues or novel psychoactive substances absent from existing reference libraries.

Section 3 of the Act imposes two requirements on the Under Secretary for Science and Technology in executing these new functions. First, the Under Secretary must follow the recommendations, guidelines, and best practices in the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (NIST AI 100-1) or any successor document. Second, the Under Secretary must establish the Directorate’s research, development, testing, evaluation, and cost-benefit analysis priorities based on the latest available threat information, specifically drugs identified in the Department of Homeland Security’s most recent Homeland Threat Assessment, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s most recent State and Territory Report on Enduring and Emerging Threats, or successor publications. Section 4 contains a rule of construction providing that nothing in the Act shall be construed to limit the authority of agencies currently involved in managing or overseeing drug-detection equipment and reference libraries. The Act authorizes the described activities but does not appropriate funds, and it prescribes no sunset, conditional effective date, or reporting requirements.
